opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Touch is, I think, one of the most underappreciated problems in robotics. People tend to assume that vision is the hard part, and vision has made enormous progress, but touch is a whole different story.

Think about what your fingertips are doing right now. You have thousands of mechanoreceptors per square centimeter, sensing pressure, vibration, texture, temperature, and slip, all at very high resolution and with very fast response times. When you pick up a paper cup of coffee, you're constantly adjusting your grip so you don't crush it or let it slide out of your hand. You do that without thinking. For a robot, that's extraordinarily difficult.

Part of the challenge is hardware. Building sensors that are sensitive, durable, cheap, and that can cover a curved, compliant surface like a fingertip is really hard. There's been nice progress, with optical tactile sensors like GelSight that use a camera behind a soft gel to capture contact deformation, but these are still bulky compared to a human finger, and they wear out.

The deeper challenge, though, is what I'd call the data problem. With vision and language, we had the internet: billions of images and documents to train on. There's no equivalent for touch. Nobody has been uploading tactile data to the web. So the large models that have been so successful elsewhere don't have that ocean of data to learn from when it comes to contact and force.

And then there's the physics. Contact is fundamentally chaotic. Tiny differences in friction, in the surface microstructure, in exactly where a finger makes contact, can lead to very different outcomes. That makes it hard to simulate accurately, which limits how much we can rely on simulation to generate training data.

So I tend to be a bit of a contrarian here. I think the hype around humanoid robots often underestimates how far we are from humanlike dexterity. I call it Moravec's paradox in action: the things that are easy for us, like picking up a glass, are incredibly hard for robots. I'm optimistic we'll make steady progress, combining better sensors, clever engineering, and learning, but I think it'll take longer than many people expect, and I'd like us to be honest about that.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So touch is, I think, one of the most underappreciated problems in robotics. We've made enormous progress in vision, partly because cameras got cheap and we had billions of images on the internet to learn from. Touch has neither of those advantages. There's no internet of tactile data. Nobody's been uploading what it feels like to pick up a wine glass.

And the human sense of touch is extraordinary. Your fingertips have thousands of mechanoreceptors sensing pressure, vibration, shear, temperature. Your skin is compliant, it deforms around objects, and your brain integrates all of that in real time with almost no conscious effort. When you reach into your pocket for your keys, you're doing something that's still very hard for the best robots in the world.

The hardware side is tough. Tactile sensors tend to be fragile, they wear out, they're hard to manufacture at scale, and they're hard to wire. You can't easily cover a whole hand in them the way skin covers yours. There's been nice work, GelSight-style sensors with cameras looking at a deformable gel, for example, but those are bulky and they sit on fingertips, not everywhere.

Then there's the data problem. Even with good sensors, you need a lot of experience to learn from, and collecting that in the physical world is slow and expensive. This is something I've thought a lot about with Dex-Net, where we got around it partly by using simulation and physics models of grasping rather than waiting for a robot to fumble with millions of real objects. But simulating contact is notoriously hard. Friction, deformation, those tiny slips, they're exactly the things that matter for touch and exactly what simulators get wrong.

So my honest view is that I'm skeptical we'll replicate human touch anytime soon, and I'm not sure we need to. Robots don't have to do things the way we do. A lot of what touch gives humans can be approximated with good vision, compliant grippers, force sensing at the wrist, and clever algorithms that are robust to uncertainty. That's been a theme of my work for a long time, embracing uncertainty rather than trying to eliminate it.

But for the hard cases, the dexterous manipulation of deformable objects, folding laundry, handling food, assisting someone in a hospital, I think touch is going to be the bottleneck. And that's a good reminder, when people talk about humanoid robots being right around the corner, that there's this gap between what looks impressive in a demo and what's actually hard. I call it a kind of Moravec's paradox in reverse. The things a two-year-old does effortlessly are still at the frontier.

astra-6.text:
Touch is one of those things that we take for granted until we try to build a robot that can do it. If you reach into your pocket and find your keys, you’re sensing pressure, texture, and motion, and adjusting your fingers as you go. It feels effortless, but there’s a tremendous amount happening there.

With robots, part of the challenge is building the sensors. You want sensitivity across the surface of the fingers, and you also want something durable enough to keep working through repeated contact. But sensing is only part of it. What does the robot do with those signals? If an object starts to slip, how should it change its grip? If it squeezes harder, will it damage the object?

So I think we have to treat touch as part of a loop between sensing and action. You touch something, move a little, and learn more about it. The goal isn’t necessarily to reproduce every aspect of human skin. It’s to give the robot enough useful feedback to handle objects reliably, even when it doesn’t know exactly what it’s holding.

sol-6.1.text:
Touch is one of those things that we take for granted until we try to reproduce it in a robot. When you pick up a glass, you’re sensing where your fingers make contact, how much pressure you’re applying, and whether it’s beginning to slip. And you’re adjusting all of that without consciously thinking about it.

For a robot, there are several problems wrapped together. You need sensors that can detect those signals, you need to integrate them into a hand that’s robust enough to use, and then you need algorithms that can turn the signals into useful actions. Having lots of measurements doesn’t automatically mean you know what you’re touching or how to respond.

I think the really interesting challenge is connecting touch with action. A robot can move a finger to learn something about an object, or adjust its grip to see whether it has a secure hold. So touch isn’t just a passive stream of information. It’s part of a continuous process of acting, sensing, and correcting. Getting that loop to work reliably is a very substantial challenge.
